certainty_reasoning: Charles Parker's own testimony includes sleeping at Taylor's with his brother and, per Hyde's editorial bracket, 'positive evidence as to the commission of acts of gross indecency at Taylor's rooms in Chapel Street,' though the bracket does not name the partner and Grain's cross elicited Parker's Bow Street statement that at Chapel Street Taylor 'did nothing to me, and I did nothing to him.'
date_label: 1893 – August 1894 (association ended at the Fitzroy Street raid)
summary: Taylor picked the Parker brothers up at the St James's Restaurant bar early in 1893 and brokered them to Wilde; Charles slept at Taylor's Little College Street rooms, stayed a fortnight at his Chapel Street rooms, and remained in Taylor's orbit until both were arrested (and discharged) in the Fitzroy Street raid of August 1894, after which Parker enlisted. Taylor was convicted of gross indecency on the count concerning Charles at his May 1895 trial.

sources.quote: In what way?—He called attention to the prostitutes who frequent Piccadilly Circus and remarked, "I can't understand sensible men wasting their money on painted trash like that. Many do, though. But there are a few who know better. Now, you could get money in a certain way easily enough if you cared to." I understood to what Taylor alluded and made a coarse reply. I am obliged to ask you what it was you actually said?—I do not like to say. You were less squeamish at the time, I dare say. I ask you for the words?—I said that if any old gentleman with money took a fancy to me, I was agreeable. I was agreeable. I was terribly hard up. What did Taylor say?—He laughed and said that men far cleverer, richer and better than I preferred things of that kind. After giving Taylor our address we parted. Did Taylor mention the prisoner Wilde?—Not at that time. Where did you first meet Wilde?—Taylor asked us to visit him (Taylor) next day at Little College Street. We went the next morning. He said he could introduce us to a man who was good for plenty of money, and that we were to meet him (Taylor) at the St. James's bar.
sources.context: Charles Parker's examination-in-chief by Mr. C. F. Gill, Regina v. Wilde and Taylor, 26 April 1895, continuing directly from the previous page, which ends 'He spoke about men.' Parker had just testified that Taylor 'came up and spoke to us' at the St James's Restaurant bar and 'was an entire stranger'.
sources.supports: How the two men met and what was proposed, in the participant's own sworn words: Taylor's approach at the bar, his proposition quoted verbatim by Parker, Parker's answer that 'if any old gentleman with money took a fancy to me, I was agreeable', and Taylor's invitation to Little College Street with the offer to introduce 'a man who was good for plenty of money'. The plainest first-hand characterization of the connection.

sources.quote: I remember subsequently going with my brother to 13 Little College Street. We slept there with Taylor. … [Witness here related proposals said to have been made by Taylor for the commission of indecencies to which the witness would not consent. Witness gave positive evidence as to the commission of acts of gross indecency at Taylor's rooms in Chapel Street.] Examination continued—I stayed with Taylor at Chapel Street for about a fortnight. Wilde used to call there, and the same thing occurred as at the Savoy.

sources.quote: Taylor told us on that occasion that he had gone through a form of marriage with a youth named Mason. Did he say who acted as the woman?—Yes; he said he did; that he was in woman's dress, and that they had a wedding breakfast.

These are the two sentences elided from the preceding quote. Taylor's Chapel Street ceremony with Charles Mason is the marriage the Crown returned to repeatedly.

sources.quote: [Soon afterwards the Solicitor-General came into Court and, after consulting with his junior counsel, Mr. Gill, said that, as far as the prosecution was concerned, they would take the verdict given by the jury upon counts 8 and 9. Mr. Grain, on behalf of Taylor, concurred.] … The Clerk of Arraigns—Gentlemen, do you find the prisoner at the bar guilty of having committed an act of gross indecency? The Foreman—Guilty.

sources.quote: [Witness, after some hesitation, recalled the names of Mason, the two Parkers, and Sidney Mavor. When pressed he added the name of Harrington.]
sources.context: Alfred Taylor cross-examined by the Solicitor-General on which men had shared his bedroom, Taylor's trial, 21 May 1895; Hyde's editorial bracket. Taylor added, on the same page, that he had not accosted the Parkers but was introduced to them by Harrington at the St James's bar - which contradicts Parker's evidence that Taylor 'was an entire stranger'.
sources.supports: Taylor's own admission that both Parkers were among the men who shared his bedroom
